facts.value: During the coronavirus pandemic, inaccurate information from all sides spread widely via social media.
facts.programme_association: Social and Cultural Analysis (Women and Gender Studies) - BA

facts.value: Topics subject to distortion included treatments, avoiding infection, vaccination, and public policy.
facts.programme_association: Social and Cultural Analysis (Women and Gender Studies) - BA

facts.value: Governments and others influenced social media platforms to suppress both accurate and inaccurate information in support of public policy.
facts.programme_association: Social and Cultural Analysis (Women and Gender Studies) - BA

facts.value: Heavier social media use was reportedly associated with more acceptance of conspiracy theories, leading to worse mental health and less compliance with public health recommendations.
facts.programme_association: Social and Cultural Analysis (Women and Gender Studies) - BA

facts.value: Social media platforms can serve as a breeding ground for addiction-related behaviors.
facts.programme_association: Social and Cultural Analysis (Women and Gender Studies) - BA

facts.value: Excessive use can lead to addiction-like symptoms including compulsive checking, mood modification, and withdrawal when not using social media.
facts.programme_association: Social and Cultural Analysis (Women and Gender Studies) - BA

facts.value: These symptoms can result in decreased face-to-face social interactions and contribute to the deterioration of interpersonal relationships and a sense of loneliness.
facts.programme_association: Social and Cultural Analysis (Women and Gender Studies) - BA
